claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are governed by interactions between alloying elements.
Alloying-element interactions produce microstructural differences that govern deformation and failure behavior.
The investigated initial state is single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Alloy composition and processing conditions will be varied.
Testing will be conducted at room or elevated temperatures after thermomechanical processing.
Grain size, precipitates, and defects are the proposed structural mediators.
Alloying-element interactions can cause solute-cluster formation.
Alloying-element interactions can cause precipitation of secondary phases.
Alloying-element interactions can modify grain-boundary structure.
Solute clustering, secondary-phase precipitation, and grain-boundary modification change strength, ductility, and fracture toughness.
Specific combinations of alloying elements will increase both strength and ductility through an optimized microstructure.
The equiatomic quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy will serve as the comparison baseline.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase FCC alloys and may not generalize to other crystal structures or alloy systems.
Atom-probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy will be used to characterize microstructure.
Tensile and fracture-toughness tests will measure mechanical properties.
The hypothesis will be falsified if composition variation neither affects microstructure nor correlates with mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is framed as applying to single-phase FCC alloys, but the proposed mechanism includes precipitation of secondary phases. It does not specify whether such precipitates are transient, nanoscale, or sufficiently limited for the material still to be classified as single-phase.
